In the Lisbon office, Marta had kept two mail slots a day, at eleven and at four, for three weeks, and her code was better for it. Then Rafael, who worked on the payment team, caught her in the corridor. "Last Thursday a server alarm was in my message to you at nine and you saw it at eleven," he said. "Nothing burned, but I was sweating."

Marta thought about it. She did not want to go back to a beeping inbox. That evening she wrote to the team: "I still read email at eleven and four. For anything urgent, call or text this number. If it isn't urgent, it waits." She put the number on the shared page and silenced her alerts again. The next week Rafael called once, at noon, about an outage, and Marta answered on the second ring. The rest of her mornings stayed quiet.

qa.a: Marta reads email at eleven and at four.

qa.a: Rafael might feel relieved to have a reliable route for real emergencies, since his worry was answered.

passage: In the university admissions office, Swati had kept two email slots a day, eleven and four, for a month. The rest of the time she worked on the scholarship files that needed long quiet reading. It worked, until last Tuesday, when a student's visa letter sat unread from noon until four and the student missed an embassy slot. Swati felt terrible. She didn't scrap the slots. Instead she printed a small card and stuck it on the office door and in her email signature: "For urgent student issues, call the desk phone, extension 214." She told Farida, who sat at the front desk, "If anyone says urgent, put them through. I'd rather be interrupted than let that happen again." On Friday the desk phone rang once. Everything else waited till four.

Subject: New way to reach me

Hi Simran and team,

Quick update. You know I've been checking email only at 10 and 3 so I can do the planning work properly. Most of you have said it's been fine. But last week Simran's message about the caterer cancelling sat in my inbox for four hours, and she had to handle it alone. That wasn't fair on her.

So I'm keeping the two slots, because they really help. But from today, if anything is urgent, a vendor dropping out, a client on the phone, someone unwell, please call my mobile; the number is in my signature. I'll pick up even in focus time. Everything else can wait for 10 or 3.

Thanks for putting up with my experiments 🙂

Reena

How does Reena seem to feel about Simran handling the caterer alone?
qa.a: Reena feels guilty and a bit uneasy, saying it wasn't fair on Simran.

qa.q: What else could Reena add to make the rule clearer?
qa.a: A few examples of what isn't urgent, so the team knows when a call is right and when to wait for the slot.

qa.a: Simran likely feels relieved and heard, knowing she won't be left alone with the next emergency.

grounding: The team lead keeps the email slots but shares a phone number for urgent matters, protecting focus without blocking emergencies.
